sections.h2: What does an Illinois quitclaim deed actually transfer?
sections.html:
An Illinois quitclaim deed passes to the grantee whatever interest the grantor holds on the day of signing, and nothing beyond that. Under 765 ILCS 5/10, a deed in the statutory form is a good conveyance, release and quit claim of "all the then existing legal or equitable rights of the grantor" in the described premises. Title the grantor picks up afterward stays behind unless the deed adds words expressing that intention.

That limit explains where the form gets used in Illinois. It suits transfers between people who already know the ownership history, such as co-owners or relatives. A buyer from the open market gets only what the seller owns, and the statutory form contains no promise about the quality of the title.

sections.h2: What does the Illinois statutory quitclaim form say?
sections.html:
The form names the grantor and the consideration, then says the grantor will "convey and quit claim" to the grantee "all interest" in the described real estate in a named county, followed by a date and signature. The statute asks that party names be typed or printed under the signatures and that the page leave a blank space of 3 1/2 inches by 3 1/2 inches for the recorder. Leaving out either detail does not affect the validity of the deed.

A deed drawn on this pattern normally carries these items:

  • The grantor's name and place of residence
  • The grantee's name or names
  • The consideration stated in the deed
  • The property's legal description plus the Illinois county where it sits
  • The date and the grantor's signature

sections.h2: What must be filed with a deed at the Illinois recorder?
sections.html:
A transfer declaration has to go in with the deed. The rule sits in section 31-25 of the Property Tax Code: the declaration is presented with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. One seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents, must sign. Apart from deeds covered by section 31-45, a recorder turns away any deed that arrives alone.

The form asks for the stated value, the parcel number, the legal description, the type of deed, the address, whether the parties are related and any homestead exemptions shown on the latest tax bill. According to the state revenue agency's own transfer tax page that Form PTAX-203 can be completed in MyDec when the county participates, and that other counties use fill-in forms. Once the deed is on record, section 31-30 sends the declaration on to the assessor's office, which is how the sale price reaches the county.

sections.h2: How much is the Illinois transfer tax on a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
Illinois taxes the privilege of transferring title at a rate of fifty cents per $500 block of the value shown on the declaration, with any leftover fraction counted as a full block, according to 35 ILCS 200/31-10. If the document states that the property passes subject to a mortgage, the unpaid mortgage balance comes out of the tax base. Liability exists even when no document is recorded.

Local layers can sit on top. The Cook County Clerk's transfer fees page prints the state and county rates below, and lets a user look up any municipality in Cook. Outside Cook, call the recorder for the county and ask which local rates apply.

sections.h2: Which Illinois deeds are exempt from transfer tax?
sections.html:
Section 31-45 lists the exempt deeds and trust documents. Several of them come up with quitclaims:

  • Deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100
  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a deed already recorded, with no additional consideration
  • Deeds of partition
  • Deeds issued to a mortgage holder in foreclosure or in a transfer in lieu of foreclosure
  • Tax deeds
  • Deeds that release property held as security for a debt

Exempt does not always mean excused from paperwork. For some categories, including actual exchanges of real estate, the statute says the deed is still not exempt from filing the declaration.

sections.h2: What does Cook County charge to record an Illinois deed?
sections.html:
Cook County prices a deed, listed as Document Class 1, at $107. The Clerk's recording fee page splits that into a $55 county recording fee, a $23 GIS fee, a $10 document storage fee, an $18 State Rental Housing Support Fee and a $1 non-government filer fee. Filers not subject to the state fee pay $19 less. Recording by mail with return adds $5 per document.

Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026, adds a fee exemption to section 10: a quitclaim recorded only to reflect a legal name change, where one individual or the same group appears on both sides, pays no recording fees. Fee schedules in other Illinois counties are set locally, so ask the county recorder before mailing a deed.

sections.h2: Where does the transfer declaration go once the deed is on file?
sections.html:
Section 31-30 says the recorder never records the declaration itself. The deed's document number is written on it, and a copy travels to the county assessor or supervisor of assessments inside 30 days of receipt. That office adds the latest assessed value for each parcel, then forwards the batch to the state revenue agency by a deadline tied either to receipt or to the close of the prior year's appeal session, whichever is later.

The assessor may keep a copy to help decide the proper valuation of the transferred property and of other parcels in the county. A quitclaim between relatives for a stated price of a few dollars therefore still leaves a record at the assessor's office, and the figures on the declaration should match the deed.

sections.h2: Does a quitclaim deed work when you want to sell an Illinois house?
sections.html:
It works when the person signing actually owns the interest being sold, because the buyer receives only that interest. Before you sign, ask whichever title company runs the closing which deed form it will take for your Illinois property.

Gather these for the recorder:

  • The signed and dated deed with the blank space reserved for the recorder
  • The completed transfer declaration, signed by a seller and a buyer or their agents
  • The transfer tax, where the transfer is not exempt
  • The county recording fee

An owner selling an inherited or jointly held house as it stands can raise the deed question early with the buyer's side, so the paperwork is settled well ahead of closing day.

faqs.q: How does an Illinois quitclaim differ from a warranty deed?
faqs.a: It differs in what it carries. The statutory quitclaim form conveys the grantor's then existing legal or equitable rights, and it does not extend to title acquired later unless the deed adds words saying so. The statute for the quitclaim form contains no promise about the quality of title.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax on an Illinois quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The Cook County Clerk's table lists the seller as the party liable for both the state and the Cook County tax. Outside Cook, contact the county recorder to learn who is liable and whether a local tax applies.

faqs.q: Is the transfer tax owed if the deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 31-10 says the tax is due whether or not a document is recorded, and it applies to transfers made through one or several related transactions.

faqs.q: Can I record a quitclaim deed just to change the name on my title?
faqs.a: Yes. The recording carries no recording fees when the sole purpose is to reflect a legal name change and the grantor is also the grantee under a new name. The exemption comes from Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026.

faqs.q: How soon must the transfer declaration be filed?
faqs.a: With the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. The declaration needs a signature from at least one seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents.
